reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .371 xwOBA and .501 xSLG say the contact quality is genuine: he's barreling 13.3% of balls and going hard 49.0% of the time, which is where a .563 projected slug comes from. The problem is a 33.6% chase rate that lives in the bottom quarter of the league, paired with a 26.2% strikeout rate that could blunt the counting stats if pitchers learn to expand the zone on him. What saves the profile is that 11.6% walk rate, because he's hunting pitches he can damage and taking the rest, so when he makes contact it matters, and the 29.6 ft/s sprint speed turns singles into doubles and outs into stolen bases at a rate that covers some of the swing-and-miss. If the chase rate stays where it is and he keeps finding those barrels, the projection of 44 home runs, 37 steals, and a .932 OPS across 723 plate appearances is well within reach; if pitchers tighten the zone and the strikeouts spike, he becomes a volatile power-speed threat who costs you batting average.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirteen-point-two percent barrels with a .351 xwOBA and .482 xSLG tells you the contact quality is doing the work, not volume luck — he's squaring balls up at an elite rate even though his hard-hit percentage sits at 39.1%, right around the middle of the league, which means the barrel shape is about angle and timing rather than pure brute force. The projection's 35 home runs across a full 703 PA season flows naturally from that profile. At 22, the whole thing hinges on whether the 26.8% whiff rate and 31.0% chase rate stay manageable as pitchers attack him harder; if those tick up, the barrel rate almost certainly follows them down, and this becomes a second-division corner rather than a frontline one. If the contact quality holds, he's a genuine run producer at the big-league level.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is almost comically stacked on both sides: a .401 xwOBA with a 15.8% barrel rate at the plate, and a 2.73 xERA with a 30.4% whiff rate on the mound. The one friction point in the hitting profile is a 31.3% whiff rate, which is where pitchers attack him and occasionally find success, but a 13.3% walk rate absorbs a lot of that damage and keeps the on-base number (.381 projected) from sliding. On the pitching side, the chase rate sits at 30.0%, which is roughly league average, meaning the 27.9% strikeout rate leans heavily on the 98.1 mph fastball and that spin doing the work once hitters are in the zone. The whole profile hinges on whether the Dodgers actually use him as a pitcher this year; if they do, you're holding two legitimate first-division contributors in one roster spot.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The exit velocity is 94.4 mph, which puts him in the 99th percentile, and the contact he makes is genuinely elite — a 14.9% barrel rate, 52.3% hard-hit rate, an xwOBA of .368. The problem is that he makes contact roughly two-thirds of the time he swings, and a 27.2% strikeout rate means a lot of those thunderous exit velocities never happen. The projection (.277/.357/.489, 26 HR, 28 SB) reflects a player whose floor is essentially set by the power and speed, but whose ceiling is gated by whether the 11.0% walk rate is enough to offset all that swing-and-miss. If the whiff rate doesn't come down, this is a high-variance everyday shortstop who'll cost you in batting average and strikeouts but more than pay you back in the counting categories.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power split is the whole tension here: a 20.7% barrel rate and 95.2 mph average exit velocity that both max out the percentile chart, sitting alongside a 28.3% strikeout rate that ranks near the bottom of the league. Wood makes extraordinary contact when he connects, and he doesn't chase, a 21.9% chase rate is elite, but the 30.4% whiff rate means pitchers who can generate swing-and-miss in the zone will keep the strikeouts high. The .417 xwOBA and .578 xSLG say the damage is real enough in quality that the strikeouts don't sink him; his 17.0% walk rate is the structural support, keeping him on base even through the swing-and-miss spells. If he ever tightens contact in the zone without losing the barrel rate, the projection's .918 OPS looks conservative.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact grades are doing most of the heavy lifting here — .296 xBA and a 54.1% hard-hit rate place him at the extreme right end of the quality-of-contact curve, and the projection's .280 AVG actually trails what the underlying contact says he should hit. Twenty-four home runs and 35 stolen bases in 706 projected plate appearances is a counting-stat haul that most lineups are built around. The one soft spot in the profile is discipline: his 26.6% whiff rate sits below league average and his 8.9% walk rate is unremarkable, so the ceiling here depends on whether he tightens the zone enough to let that elite contact quality compound into an OPS north of .802 across a full season. If the contact translates cleanly and the legs stay healthy, this is a legitimate multi-category force; if the whiff rate creeps and the walks don't grow, you're looking at a very good player whose raw tools suggest something more.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile. Ninety-two walks across A+ & A at 18 years old, an 18 BB%, translating to a 12.6% MLB-equivalent rate when most big leaguers sit around 8.5%, is the kind of plate discipline that barely exists at this level from teenagers. Add 60 stolen bases and a .404 OBP and you're looking at a profile built around getting on base and moving, with the .195 ISO suggesting the power is developing rather than arrived, and the translated ISO of .132 trailing the MLB average, so the question the whole ceiling hinges on is whether that gap closes as he physically matures. If it does, everyday shortstop is a real outcome; if the power stalls, the elite walk rates and wheels still point toward a useful regular, just one whose value lives almost entirely in OBP and speed.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The contact hasn't come back yet, but the underlying quality is quietly loud. His 91.8 mph average exit velocity and 48.0% hard-hit rate sit well above average, yet a 27.1% whiff rate suppresses the batting average enough that his xBA lands at just .250 — the ball-in-play outcomes are fine, the contact rate is the leak. What saves the profile is an 11.4% walk rate and 29.7 ft/s sprint speed, which between them manufacture value the slash line undersells; he projects at .242/.336/.469 with 22 home runs and 24 stolen bags across 684 plate appearances, a genuine everyday contributor even if he never fully solves the strikeout problem. Tighten the whiff rate modestly and the power-speed combination with that walk discipline becomes a top-of-the-order profile; leave it where it is and you have a regular whose value lives in everything that happens around the batting average.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost entirely real and the chase rate is almost entirely a problem. Caglianone's 93.1 mph average exit velocity and 54.4% hard-hit rate sit near the top of the league, and an .xSLG of .505 says the raw power translates when he makes contact. But a 39.2% chase rate and 5.9% walk rate tell you the profile lives or dies on whether pitchers eventually learn they can expand the zone against him and he never adjusts. If the approach holds roughly where it is, something in the neighborhood of 26 home runs with an .821 OPS in a full season is a reasonable outcome; if the chase rate climbs as scouting reports deepen, you're left with a loud exit-velo profile attached to a hitter who can't reach base enough to make it count.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate jumps off the page, 11.5 K/9 at AA translating to 9.1 at the MLB level, but the walk rate is where this profile gets complicated. Fifty-two free passes in 98 innings at AA produces a BB/9 of 4.8, and the translation barely moves it, landing at 4.6 while the MLB average sits at 3.2. The K-BB% translates to 13.0 at the major-league level, right where the average falls, which is the quiet problem: elite strikeout stuff is being neutralized by the control, and nothing in this profile suggests the walks are an aberration rather than the shape of the pitcher. If the command sharpens, you have a rotation piece; if it doesn't, this is a depth arm cycling through the upper minors.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The ERA and the xERA are telling two very different stories, and the Statcast profile takes the pessimist's side. His 3.13 ERA projection sits alongside a 4.36 xERA, and the underlying numbers explain the gap: a 21.0% strikeout rate and 9.6% walk rate leave almost no margin, yet hitters are making soft enough contact, 87.1 mph average exit velocity and a Hard-Hit% of 33.0%, that the surface results have stayed clean. The contact-suppression is doing real work, but if that softness regresses toward what a .321 xwOBA implies, the ERA follows it up fast. King can be a useful mid-rotation piece for San Diego across those 189 projected innings, but this profile hinges almost entirely on whether the soft contact is a repeatable skill or a stretch of fortune catching up with ordinary swing-and-miss stuff.

reports.name: Harry Ford
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Ford has drawn 45 walks against 65 strikeouts across 257 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and that 18% walk rate translates to 12.8% at the MLB level — genuine plate discipline at a position where patience alone buys roster value. The problem is everything else: a .223 average, four home runs, and an ISO of .112 at AAA that translates to .116 at the MLB level, well short of what catchers typically need to hold a lineup spot. If the eye stays and contact ticks up enough to leverage those walks into real OBP, he's a backup catcher with an unusually patient approach worth keeping; if the bat stalls where it is, the walks sustain a career without earning him a regular role.

reports.name: Devin Taylor
reports.published_report: The .414 BABIP is doing a lot of work here, and that's the whole conversation. Devin Taylor is hitting .316/.419/.503 across AAA & AA & A+ in 608 plate appearances, with 92 walks keeping the on-base number honest even as 158 strikeouts signal the contact profile is fragile. reports.name: Joey Cantillo
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Cantillo generates whiffs at a 29.7% clip, a genuinely above-average rate, but his 11.7% walk rate is where the profile caves, sitting in the 14th percentile and dragging an otherwise functional contact-suppression profile toward mediocrity. The xERA of 4.04 and dead-center xwOBA of .310 tell you exactly what he is right now: a pitcher who misses bats without being able to locate well enough to make those misses matter. If the zone command tightens and the walk rate comes down even modestly, the strikeout ability gives him a real mid-rotation floor; if it doesn't, 159.8 projected innings of 1.47 WHIP ball is a back-end starter you're managing around rather than building around.

reports.name: Pete Hansen
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing keeping this profile from being purely organizational filler. Across AAA & A this season, Hansen has posted a 3.4 BB/9 that translates to 3.5 at the MLB level, right where league control concerns start, while his strikeout rate translates to a 7.7 K/9 against an MLB average of 8.6, and that gap is where the ceiling collapses. Ninety-three strikeouts in 99.4 innings sounds workable until you see that the command advantage is carrying almost all the weight, and a 1.4 WHIP across those two levels says even the command isn't clean enough to paper over the swing-and-miss shortfall. If the walk rate holds and tightens, he's a depth arm who can eat innings without embarrassing himself; if it doesn't, there's nothing else in the profile to lean on.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells the real story here, and it's not a comfortable one. His xERA sits at 4.12 and his BB% at 10.1%, a combination that makes a projected 3.35 ERA feel like it leans heavily on contact management — the 6.1% barrel rate is genuine, but soft contact suppression is a shaky foundation when the walk rate lives in the bottom third of the league. The 20.7% strikeout rate doesn't generate enough margin for error on those baserunners, and the role split across 106.7 projected innings with 11 holds and just a single quality start suggests Milwaukee is using him as a bulk/hybrid arm rather than trusting him to start games. If the barrel suppression slips, he's a back-end reliever with a high walk rate and not much else.

reports.name: Kane Kepley
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. Across AA & A+, Kane Kepley has drawn 118 walks against 85 strikeouts in 566 plate appearances, a 21% walk rate that translates to 15% at the big-league level while the MLB average sits closer to half that, and that gap is the engine of everything. The 64 stolen bases say he knows how to spend a baserunning edge, but the MLB-equivalent ISO sits at .125, below average for the level he'd be entering, so the ceiling is capped by what happens when pitchers decide he's not going to hurt them with the bat. He's either a high-OBP bench piece who earns playing time with a glove and a green light, or he's a fringe roster name whose walk rate doesn't survive the jump if pitchers attack the zone and he can't punish them for it.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the loudest thing in this profile: 33.4% gets hitters expanding off the zone at a clip that sits at the 80th percentile, and that's what props up a 3.68 xERA that the projection doesn't quite trust. The 4.09 ERA across a projected 127.9 innings suggests the underlying quality is real enough but fragile at the margins, and the barrel rate of 8.7% is the specific threat — when hitters do make contact, Drohan gets hurt more than most of his xERA peers would. His 2442 rpm fastball spin is an elite shape attribute that explains why the chase numbers play, but the strikeout rate at 23.8% is middling, so the profile leans on location and movement over pure swing-and-miss. If the chase rate regresses or the barrel rate climbs, this becomes a backend arm in a crowded rotation fight rather than a quiet mid-rotation contributor, and that's exactly where the projection lands: useful innings, nothing more.

reports.name: Axiel Plaz
reports.published_report: The A+ line is genuinely pretty — .305/.389/.513 through 412 plate appearances, with 18 home runs and a 10% walk rate sitting comfortably alongside a 17% strikeout rate. At the catcher position, that contact-and-patience combination is unusual enough to notice. But the MLB translation is where the ceiling conversation gets complicated: A+ power at .207 ISO softens to .144 at the big-league level, landing just below a league-average mark of .150, and the walk rate follows a similar path downward. If the bat speed and recognition that produce those A+ results translate cleanly, a real question across two to three years and several levels, you get a functional big-league catcher with a serviceable floor; if the hit tool fades when pitching gets sharper, what's left is organizational depth behind the plate.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the command is the problem, and right now the problem is winning. Across 61.7 innings at A+, he's punched out 73 hitters at 10.7 K/9, but 51 walks at 7.4 BB/9 have produced a 1.8 WHIP and a 6.70 ERA that leaves almost no argument for the present. Translate that profile to MLB-equivalent and the strikeouts land near league average while the walk rate lands at 6.4, roughly double what big-league starters typically allow, and a K-BB% of 8.6% against the 13.5% norm tells you exactly how much the free passes are eating the upside. The entire profile hinges on whether the walks compress as he matures, because if they don't, the strikeout ceiling has nowhere to go and he's a depth arm by ceiling and floor.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card, and it's also the problem. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell has drawn 113 walks in 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and he's added 27 stolen bases and 23 home runs on top of it, a legitimately unusual combination for a catcher at 21. But the .234 average against a .346 BABIP tells you the strikeouts aren't disappearing, and when that contact rate translates to an MLB-equivalent 36.8% K%, what survives the jump is a 15.4% walk rate propped up against average power at .152 ISO. The whole profile hinges on whether the discipline holds as pitchers locate better, because if the strikeouts climb and the walks compress even modestly, the .234 average becomes the story rather than the footnote. If it works, he's a patient, borderline-average offensive catcher who runs; if it doesn't, the bench is the ceiling.

Across AAA & AA in 2026, Mullins has run a 13.1 K/9 and owns 130 strikeouts in 89.7 innings, which translates to a 10.0 K/9 at the MLB-equivalent level, but his 5.1 BB/9 follows him there too, coming out to 4.8 where big-league hitters will find it even more damaging. Depth ceiling, depth floor.

If the contact improves and the BABIP settles somewhere defensible, he's a bench piece with real baserunning value; if it doesn't, the speed alone won't carry him past organizational depth.
